newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW - APPLE SEES ASIA GROWTH MOMENTUM.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - APPLE SEES ASIA GROWTH MOMENTUM.

text.p: Apple Computer Inc sees its growth momentum in Asia continuing with its focus on publishing and learning markets, a senior company official said on Thursday.
"There is plenty of opportunity for upside. The overall trend is definitely for growth," Steve Vamos, and managing director of Apple Asia Pacific, told Reuters in an interview.
Vamos, in Singapore for a MacWorld Exposition opening on Friday, said that the company's third fiscal quarter revenue ended June 1997 in Asia had risen 12 percent over the previous quarter.

He said Asian growth was due to Apple's focus on publishing and learning markets. And the region was a market made for Apple with the huge interest of governments and parents in education and the big consumption of newspapers and reading, he said.
Asia "should absolutely be the fastest growing" for Apple, he added.
Asian revenue in fiscal 1997, which ends in September, would be higher than 1995, when Apple's worldwide revenue was at its peak of US$11 billion, he said.
In fiscal 1997, Apple has been concentrating on mid to high-end products for the publishing sector after selling mainly low-end products previously, he said.
"I think our revenue this year could be comparable to last, he said. Asian sales in 1996 were about 15 percent higher than in 1995, Vamos said. He declined to be more specific.
Apple was looking at a broader presence in Asia in terms of more investment in marketing and sales, Vamos said.
It would continue to use a Singapore facility for manufacturing for the region but would focus skills and infrastructure in more than building a box.
This includes new ways to source components, new processes like build-to-order and working closer with distributors and assemblers to meet customers' needs and to reduce cost.

Apple would honour existing contracts with clone-makers who have licensed its operating systems and was in the progress of renegotiating contracts for its new Mac OS8 operating system and yet-to-be-launched Rhapsody, he said.
Apple wants to ensure the licensing programme would increase the MacIntosh business, he said.
While the tie-up with Microsoft Corp was seen as a major boost to Apple, it could not guarantee it was the end of downsizing for the company, Vamos said.
Microsoft is investing US$150 million in Apple and has promised to develop major product upgrades for Apple's MacinTosh operating system for five years.
Microsoft's Internet Explorer would also become Apple's default Web browser but does not exclude use of Netscape Communications Corp's products.
"We still have a few quarters ahead in getting the focus and building the strength back in the business." Vamos said.

On its Singapore cutbacks in recent months, he said: "It is not about volume downturn but about leveraging industry infrastructure. We have to recognise we can't do everything in house and be competitive with specialised focused players in the industry."
In Singapore, Apple has laid off some 350 workers in the last three months and closed its design centre and print circuit board manufacturing.
It still has more than 600 staff in Singapore.
